red.focus: See how economic conditions affect legal rights in practice
red.summary: A right can exist on paper while being costly or difficult to exercise. Learn the difference between formal protection and the real choices available to the person holding it.
checklist: I can identify transaction costs of enforcing a right
I can explain why access affects practical protection
I can distinguish wealth from entitlement

sections.title: Rights Have Practical Costs
sections.body_md: A person may have a legally valid claim for a small unpaid wage but lack money for a lawyer or time to attend court. Filing fees, travel and delay can make the right difficult to enforce. Economists call some of these transaction costs: resources spent making an exchange or enforcing an arrangement. The legal right remains real, but the person's practical access is weaker. Studying those costs helps design procedures that protect people who cannot afford lengthy litigation.

sections.title: Price Is Not Justice
sections.body_md: Suppose a wealthy business can pay a modest regulatory fine without changing its behavior. The fine may be legally valid yet fail to prevent harm. Conversely, the same amount could be devastating to a low-income individual. An economic analysis can examine incentives and distribution, but it cannot decide fairness by income alone. Legal rights and proportionality constraints must still be identified. The purpose is to understand how people actually respond to rules and how those responses affect protection.

sections.title: Who Can Use the System?
sections.body_md: Two people may hold the same formal tenancy right but have very different access to records, representation or transportation. An outcome analysis should ask what prevents people from invoking the protection. Some solutions are procedural, such as clearer notices or low-cost dispute resolution; others involve legal aid or administrative enforcement. Economic insight matters when it exposes obstacles to effective freedom. Law serves people, not merely the appearance of equal treatment on paper.

yellow.focus: Compare efficiency and distribution when rights are allocated
yellow.summary: Legal rules assign benefits, burdens and bargaining power. Learn why an arrangement that maximizes total measured wealth may still leave some persons unjustly disadvantaged.
checklist: I can distinguish efficiency from distribution
I can identify parties bearing external costs
I can consider whether voluntary bargaining is realistic

sections.title: Total Gain Is Not the Whole Story
sections.body_md: A new zoning rule increases citywide property values but displaces a small low-income neighborhood. An aggregate calculation may show net monetary gains while ignoring who benefits and who bears the loss. Efficiency asks how resources are used; distribution asks how benefits and burdens are shared. Legal systems may protect rights that cannot simply be traded for greater total wealth. An honest economic analysis presents both dimensions rather than hiding one inside the other.

sections.title: Bargaining Is Not Costless
sections.body_md: Imagine two neighbors disagree about factory noise. If rights are clear and negotiation is easy, they may find a mutually acceptable arrangement. But large numbers of affected residents, incomplete information and unequal power can prevent agreement. Transaction costs matter. The Coasean insight about bargaining under idealized conditions is useful precisely because actual legal systems rarely satisfy every assumption. The law must choose rules with attention to real institutions and rights.

sections.title: External Costs Matter
sections.body_md: A firm producing a valuable product may impose air pollution on people who did not agree to accept it. Economists call that an externality: a cost or benefit borne by others outside the relevant transaction. Legal tools such as liability rules, regulation or taxes can address some external effects. Their justification depends on evidence and applicable legal authority. The fact that a business is profitable does not establish that all relevant costs have been considered.

orange.focus: Analyze unequal bargaining and behavioral constraints on rights
orange.summary: Advanced economic analysis challenges the assumption that every agreement reflects informed, unconstrained choice. Examine information asymmetry, market power and behavioral framing.
checklist: I can identify unequal information in rights-related decisions
I can explain how default rules influence choice
I can distinguish behavioral description from legal justification

sections.title: Agreement Can Hide Information Gaps
sections.body_md: A consumer clicks acceptance of complex software terms without knowing how their data will be used. The company understands the technology and risks better than the consumer. Information asymmetry may weaken the assumption that the transaction reflects equally informed choice. Law can respond through disclosure, default protections or mandatory limits where authorized. An analyst should consider how well disclosure actually works instead of treating the mere presence of text as proof of understanding.

sections.title: Defaults Change Decisions
sections.body_md: People often remain with a preselected option because changing it requires attention or effort. A pension program's default enrollment or a data-sharing opt-out can therefore influence behavior without an explicit prohibition. Behavioral economics studies such patterns, but descriptive findings do not alone justify manipulating people's choices. Legal evaluation must ask whether the design respects autonomy, notice, equality and applicable consent requirements. A helpful default can also be used coercively if exit is obscure.

sections.title: Power Changes the Bargain
sections.body_md: A worker dependent on one employer or a renter in a scarce market may have limited ability to refuse unfavorable terms. A formal signature does not demonstrate equal bargaining power. Legal protections can respond through minimum standards, anti-discrimination rules, or collective processes, depending on the jurisdiction. The economic task is to identify actual alternatives, information and costs. The legal task is to determine what duties the system imposes and what remedies people can obtain.

black.focus: Defend rights-sensitive economic analysis under inequality
black.summary: At doctoral depth, evaluate welfare economics and its limitations in a legal order committed to dignity and justice. Explain why willingness to pay is an imperfect measure of rights and human needs.
checklist: I can critique monetization of nonmarket interests
I can compare efficiency and egalitarian perspectives
I can design evidence-based rights protections with accountability

sections.title: Money Is an Unequal Measure
sections.body_md: Willingness to pay can reflect income as much as the importance of a benefit. A rich person's preference may appear more valuable in a market calculation than a poor person's essential housing or safety. Cost-benefit analysis may assist policy, but its outputs must be read alongside distribution, legal rights and the limits of monetary valuation. A doctoral scholar should identify what the model omits, whose preferences are counted and what normative judgment is being made.

sections.title: Kaldor-Hicks Is Not Consent
sections.body_md: A policy can be described as potentially improving welfare if winners could compensate losers and still retain a gain. That does not mean losers were actually compensated or agreed. A doctoral analysis distinguishes potential compensation from Pareto improvement, in which no one is made worse off under the specified evaluation. It also confronts the difficulty of measuring nonmarket dignity, environmental loss and coercion. Economic criteria are tools for reasoning, not substitutes for legitimate authority.

sections.title: Design Justice-Conscious Evaluation
sections.body_md: A public legal policy should specify measurable benefits and costs, identify vulnerable groups, account for uncertainty and show how legal constraints shape permissible choices. Distributional weights or alternative evaluation methods can make assumptions explicit but cannot eliminate ethical disagreement. A defensible framework invites review, includes affected-person voices and measures actual outcomes after implementation. The goal is to use evidence to strengthen protection of lives and freedoms, not to reduce those values to one financial total.
